name: Bigtable
oneLiner: Low-latency, wide-column NoSQL for huge analytical and operational workloads.
whatItIs: Bigtable is Google Cloud's wide-column NoSQL database — the same technology that underpins Search, Maps and Gmail. It's built for enormous scale (petabytes) and very high throughput with consistent low latency, storing rows keyed by a single row key with columns grouped into families. It shines for time-series, IoT, financial ticks, and any workload with massive write/read volume and simple key-based access. It's not a document store or a general-purpose database — it's a sparse, sorted key-value/wide-column map optimised for scale and speed, and it speaks the HBase API.

inPractice.narrative: An IoT platform ingests millions of sensor readings per second. Each reading is written to Bigtable with a row key like device#timestamp, so recent data for a device is a fast contiguous range scan. Dashboards and serving apps read those ranges in milliseconds, while a Dataflow job also reads Bigtable (or its exports) to roll data into BigQuery for deep analytics. Bigtable is the high-throughput operational/time-series store; BigQuery is where the heavy analysis happens.

coreConcepts.detail: Every access is by row key or key range; the key's structure determines performance. Sequential keys (like raw timestamps) cause hotspots — good design distributes writes while keeping useful ranges contiguous.
Rows have column families containing many sparse columns; data is stored sorted by row key. It's a map, not tables with joins.
Throughput scales roughly linearly with nodes; you add nodes for more QPS. Storage and compute scale, and you can resize without downtime.
Bigtable exposes the Apache HBase API, so HBase apps and tools port over — easing migration from on-prem Hadoop.
Multi-cluster replication gives high availability and geo-distribution with eventual consistency across clusters.
Its sorted-key range scans make it ideal for time-series/IoT/financial data where you read recent windows per entity.

whenToUse: Very high-throughput reads/writes at massive (TB–PB) scale.
Time-series, IoT, financial tick and monitoring data.
Low-latency key/range lookups where you know the access pattern.
Migrating HBase/Hadoop workloads to a managed service.
Operational serving that also feeds analytics downstream.
whenNotToUse: Ad-hoc SQL analytics, joins and aggregations — use BigQuery.
Small datasets or low throughput — a node-based minimum makes it overkill (use Firestore).
Rich document queries or transactions across entities — use Firestore/Spanner.
Workloads without a clear row-key access pattern — the model punishes that.

keyFacts.label: Access
keyFacts.value: By row key or key range (no secondary indexes/joins).

pricingShape: Bigtable (provisioned) bills mainly per node-hour for the cluster's nodes plus storage per GB-month (SSD costs more than HDD) and some network. Because you pay for nodes whether or not they're busy, there's a real baseline cost — it's economical at high, steady utilisation and expensive for small or idle workloads (which is why Firestore fits low-scale better). Throughput scales with nodes, so the levers are right-sizing node count to your QPS and choosing SSD vs HDD by latency needs. Autoscaling can adjust nodes to load.
gotchas: Sequential row keys (raw timestamps, incrementing IDs) create hotspots that throttle throughput — salt/field-promote the key.
You pay per node even when idle; there's a practical minimum cost, so it's poor for small workloads.
No joins, no secondary indexes, limited transactions — model entirely around row-key access.
It's operational/serving, not an analytics engine — don't run reporting scans on it; move to BigQuery.
Schema/key design mistakes are costly to fix later because everything hinges on the row key.

equivalents.name: Amazon DynamoDB
equivalents.note: Serverless key-value/document; DynamoDB scales to zero-ish, Bigtable is node-based.

equivalents.name: Azure Cosmos DB
equivalents.note: Multi-model NoSQL; Cosmos has a wide-column (Cassandra) API among others.
